summary: Rep. Jim Jordan failed on a second House speaker ballot on Wednesday, losing 22 Republicans, two more than the day before, leaving his path to the gavel almost certainly lost. The House has been without a speaker for 15 days since Kevin McCarthy's ouster, and a bipartisan group floated giving interim speaker-pro-tempore Patrick McHenry more power to reopen the chamber. Gingrich and Boehner backed the idea while Jordan vowed to stay in the race.
one_line: Jim Jordan lost a second House speaker vote with 22 Republican defections, deepening the GOP impasse and prompting talk of empowering interim speaker Patrick McHenry.
key_facts: Jim Jordan failed on the second ballot for House speaker on Wednesday, opposed by 22 Republicans, two more than in the first round the day before.
The House had been without a speaker for 15 days since the sudden ouster of Kevin McCarthy; the House had never ousted its speaker before McCarthy.
In the Wednesday tally, 199 Republicans voted for Jordan and 212 for Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, leaving no candidate with a clear majority.
Republicans hold a 221-212 majority in the House, so Jordan must win over most of his GOP foes.

A bipartisan group of lawmakers floated giving interim speaker-pro-tempore Rep. Patrick McHenry, R-N.C., more power to reopen the House and conduct routine business, using temporary powers created after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Former GOP speakers Newt Gingrich and John Boehner backed the idea of boosting the interim speaker's role; Gingrich said he has 'no faith' Jordan can get much beyond the 200 votes he won in the first vote.
New Jordan opponent Rep. Vern Buchanan of Florida said, 'I think it's time to move on.'
Holdouts cast ballots for McCarthy, Majority Leader Steve Scalise and others, with one vote going to the retired Boehner.
Some Republicans resented being pressured by Jordan's allies and said they were threatened with primary opponents if they didn't support him.
Trump backed Jordan, saying outside a Manhattan courthouse that he would be a great speaker; Trump awarded Jordan a Medal of Freedom days after the Jan. 6 Capitol attack.
Jordan, a founding member of the Freedom Caucus and Judiciary Committee chairman, was first elected in 2006 and has few bills to his name.
Jordan denied allegations from former Ohio State wrestlers that he knew about claims they were groped by an Ohio doctor.
Hundreds of protesters gathered outside the Capitol over the Israel-Hamas war while the House was stalled.
